title: Below scientia is not yet uncertain — moral certainty still binds conscience unto death
source_text: XXXVI. Nec propterea fides, saltem ex hac parte, incerta relinquitur. Quod enim non attingit certitudinem scientiae & intelligentiae, statim tamen incertum non est. Quippe, ut ante ostensum est, certitudo quae moralis dicitur, etiamsi sit inferioris gradus, est tamen veri nominis certitudo, quae mentem securam & indubiam reddit. Nec alia requiritur ut homines ad munia & officia vitae obligentur in conscientia, & efficaciter etiam impellantur: vel usque ad vitam propriam exponendam, & mortem ultro subeundam, quod facit aliquando subditus pro principe, & pater pro liberis, quos suos esse non aliter certus est.
pass_a_gloss: Nor therefore is faith, at least on this side, left uncertain. For what does not attain the certainty of science and intelligence is not for that reason straightway uncertain. Indeed, as was shown before, the certainty which is called moral, even if of an inferior grade, is yet certainty of the true name, which renders the mind secure and undoubting. Nor is another required that men be bound in conscience to the offices and duties of life, and also be efficaciously driven — even to exposing their own life and freely undergoing death, as a subject sometimes does for his prince, and a father for his children, of whom he is not otherwise certain that they are his.
pass_b_english: Moral certainty (lower grade) still veri nominis — secure mind.
Enough for conscience-duties unto death (subject/prince; father/children).
